format.label: A memo to a CMO
format.instruction: Write it as a short internal memo to a chief marketing officer. Plain language, no jargon they would have to look up. Around 120 words.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach:
Memo to CMO — Cross-channel orchestration

The obvious move is to buy a central decision brain and let it pick the next best action everywhere. I'd skip that. No channel will hand over execution, and we can't define the objective it would optimize anyway.

I'd start smaller: a referee, not a brain. One service that every channel checks before sending, with veto power only — never telling them what to send, just whether they may. That's politically survivable and only needs an identity key and a contact log.

Then treat customer attention as a budget we allocate, like media spend.

Expect trouble: feedback from ads and service arrives late or never, identity breaks at the edges, and teams will route around a suppression rule they dislike. The hard part is agreeing what a good week looks like for a customer — that's a leadership decision, not a model.
answers.first_move: Put one suppression service in front of every outbound channel and log what it blocks for 60 days.
answers.hardest_part: There is no agreed definition of a good customer experience to optimize toward, and the people who would have to agree are paid on conflicting numbers.

answers.label: ChatGPT
answers.approach:
To: CMO
Subject: Starting cross-channel coordination

I would not begin by building a universal decision engine. The data, incentives and control needed to make one trustworthy do not yet exist.

I would start with one high-volume journey—such as onboarding or renewal—across three channels. We would create a shared customer contact record, define hard rules for conflicting offers and contact limits, and reserve a control group receiving today’s treatment. Success would be judged on margin, complaints, service demand and retention, not conversion alone.

The experiment should sit under one business owner with authority over channel budgets. We would then add channels only when their actions and outcomes can be measured reliably.

The hardest problem will not be software. It will be agreeing which outcomes matter when short-term channel targets conflict with customer value.
answers.first_move: Choose one important customer journey and give one leader authority over its channels and budget.
answers.hardest_part: The hardest part is agreeing how to trade short-term channel results against margin, service costs, fatigue and long-term customer value.

answers.label: Gemini
answers.approach: Vendors promise a central brain that decides every touchpoint across all channels. That does not work. Channel data arrives at different speeds, and your channel leaders will always fight to protect their own targets. Instead of chasing a master algorithm, I would start with basic defense: strict, universal suppression rules to stop us from hitting people with contradictory offers. Next, I would test coordination across just two channels that share fast data, like email and mobile push, funded by a single shared budget. We will run into broken attribution, lagging signals, and political friction immediately. But finding where the seams rip on two channels is useful work; trying to solve seven at once is an expensive trap.
answers.first_move: Set hard cross-channel frequency caps so we stop spamming customers before we try to coordinate what we say to them.
answers.hardest_part: You cannot optimize a single journey until you define the exact financial trade-off between an immediate sale today and customer fatigue tomorrow.

format.label: Three moves
format.instruction: Give exactly three moves, in order. One sentence each, then one sentence on what makes that move hard. Nothing else.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach:
Move 1: Make every channel write to a single contact ledger — every touch sent, suppressed, and every inbound signal, at person grain, before the send rather than in a nightly reconciliation — and treat that write as the price of admission to the customer, enforced by budget approval rather than by architecture review. What makes it hard: paid media and batch ESPs physically cannot report at the grain and latency you need, so you end up with a ledger that is exact for owned channels and probabilistic for the rest, and you have to decide early how much inference you'll tolerate in a system of record.

Move 2: Resist building a global optimizer and instead ship a constraint layer first — frequency caps, offer exclusivity, service-state suppression, and a hard "send nothing" option — because contradictory offers and over-contact are governance failures, not optimization failures, and constraints are the only decision logic channel owners will actually accept losing control over. What makes it hard: every constraint takes volume away from someone with a number to hit, so this is a quarter of negotiation per rule, and you must be able to show that suppressed sends did not cost the revenue the channel owner will claim they cost.

Move 3: Only then earn an objective function empirically, by running a permanent person-level global holdout across all channels and fitting weights on fatigue, margin, and service outcomes against what that holdout reveals, rather than convening a committee to agree on a utility function in advance. What makes it hard: a true global holdout means deliberately under-marketing real customers for long enough to see downstream value, every channel team loses attributable credit for those people, and the signal you most want — long-term value — arrives quarters after the decisions you're trying to improve.
answers.first_move: Get every channel writing every send and suppression for a person into one shared log, in real time.
answers.hardest_part: The decisions happen in milliseconds per channel, but the outcome you actually care about only becomes visible months later at a coarse grain — so the feedback loop that would teach the system is structurally slower than the system itself.

Move 2: Build a minimal shared customer-state and experimentation layer for a few high-value journeys, including identity confidence, exposure logs, eligibility, costs, outcomes, randomized holdouts, and explicit unknown states.
Hard: Identity is probabilistic, APIs and feedback are uneven, and long-term effects such as fatigue are delayed, confounded, and only partly observable.

answers.label: Gemini
answers.approach: 1. Strip delivery platforms of their autonomous scheduling and force them to act purely as stateless execution pipes governed by a central priority queue. What makes this hard is that channel teams and SaaS vendors have zero commercial or political incentive to surrender execution control to an external layer. 2. Abandon continuous global mathematical optimization and instead enforce strict, deterministic negative constraints like cross-channel cooldowns and universal suppression lists. What makes this hard is that proving suppression protects long-term value requires withholding profitable-looking messages, which marketers fight at budget review. 3. Establish a lightweight, event-driven state arbiter that makes arbitration decisions based only on immediate recency and intent signals rather than trying to model full journey graphs. What makes this hard is that network latency and delayed channel reporting mean the arbitration engine is almost always deciding on stale customer state.
answers.first_move: Take away scheduling and triggering permissions from individual channel tools so they only execute sends on command.
answers.hardest_part: Channel teams and vendors will actively fight losing execution autonomy because their budgets and compensation rely on channel-specific attribution.

format.label: Pseudocode
format.instruction: Express the approach as short annotated pseudocode. The comments should carry the reasoning; the code should carry the structure. Around 15 lines.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach:
```
# PREMISE I'D ARGUE WITH: don't build a global policy that picks the next best action.
# Channel-level models are already decent; the damage comes from collisions, fatigue and
# contradiction. So make the global layer THIN: a scarcity allocator, not a brain.

for each customer, every tick:
  state = union(channel_events)          # accept it's incomplete; version it, and let
                                         # each bid declare which facts it depends on
  attention_budget = f(fatigue_model)    # ONE budget per person, in currency, not per channel.
                                         # Currency is the point: finance can argue with a price,
                                         # they cannot argue with a propensity score.

  bids = [ch.propose(state) for ch in channels]   # channels keep their own models and ownership.
                                                  # Each bid = (payload, expected_margin, decay, exclusivity)

  if service_open(state): preempt(marketing_bids)  # non-negotiable. Service isn't a bidder,
                                                   # it's a stop condition. Most orchestration
                                                   # failures I've seen are this one rule missing.

  winners = allocate(bids, attention_budget, shadow_price)
  # shadow_price is tuned nightly until spend clears the budget. This dodges the
  # "no agreed objective function" blocker: nobody has to agree on weights,
  # they only have to accept a clearing price they can see and appeal.

  for ch in slow_lanes(paid_media):     # ad platforms can't be held back at decision time
    ch.commit(winners, horizon=6h)      # so pre-commit and accept staleness; audit drift later

  log(decision, shadow_price, state_version)   # replayability > accuracy. You will be wrong;
                                               # you need to prove WHY you were wrong.

# MEASUREMENT (the part that actually decides whether this lives):
global_holdout = 2% of people, excluded from ALL channels, not per-channel holdouts.
# Per-channel incrementality tests sum to more than reality. One person-level holdout
# is the only honest read on whether coordination beat the sum of the parts.
```
What I expect to hit: exclusivity declarations will be gamed — every channel will claim its offer is exclusive — so the bid schema needs adversarial review, not just a spec. Fatigue decay is unidentifiable from observational data; you'll have to deliberately over-contact a slice to fit it, and someone senior has to sign off on that. And the shadow price will swing wildly in the first months, which reads as "the system is broken" to channel owners who lose impressions. That's a change-management problem, and it kills more of these than the math does.
answers.first_move: Put a single person-level holdout across every channel so we can actually tell whether coordination helps.
answers.hardest_part: There is no objective function to agree on, so the system has to produce a tradeoff price that organizations can argue with rather than a hidden weighting they'll quietly route around.

format.label: A checklist
format.instruction: Give a checklist someone could actually run next quarter. Each item concrete enough to be marked done or not done. Six items at most.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach:
My honest position up front: the blocker is not the optimizer. Decision science for this is largely solved in adjacent fields (constrained assignment, bandits, scheduling). What's missing is a shared ledger of what we did to people, an empirically priced cost of contact, and a political mechanism that lets one layer say no. So I'd build the veto before the brain, and I'd resist the two obvious moves — a central "next best action" planner and an RL agent over the full journey. A planner you can't enforce is a Powerpoint, and RL over sparse, delayed, partially-observed cross-channel feedback will happily learn your attribution bugs.

Checklist for the quarter:

1. **Contact ledger live for the top three channels.** One append-only log of every outbound touch and every inbound customer event, keyed to a stable identity, with a documented latency SLA per channel. Done = you can answer "everything this person received in the last 30 days" for ≥95% of touches, within five minutes of send, from a single query. Expect to find that 20–40% of outbound (triggered service mail, app push from product teams, agent-initiated outreach) isn't in any marketing system today.

2. **Global holdout cohort stood up and defended.** 2–5% of customers excluded from all orchestration logic across every channel, identity-stable, refreshed never. Done = the cohort exists, channel teams cannot see or target it, and one exec report has been published where the headline number is cohort-vs-treated incremental margin, not channel KPIs. This is simultaneously your only trustworthy feedback signal and your only defense against four teams each claiming the same conversion.

3. **Arbitration service that only suppresses.** A pre-send call every channel makes; it returns allow/deny/defer, never "send this instead." V1 is frequency caps, conflict rules (no promo while an open service ticket exists, no acquisition offer to an existing owner), and quiet hours. Done = three channels integrated, suppression volume reported daily, and a documented override path for legal/transactional. Suppression needs no budget transfer, which is exactly why it ships and a planner doesn't.

4. **A measured price for contact pressure.** Run a frequency/pressure experiment — randomize contact budget per customer, not per campaign — and estimate the marginal contribution and the marginal unsubscribe/churn/service-cost of the Nth touch, by segment. Done = a number with a confidence interval, per segment, written down. Without this, the "agreed objective function" conversation is theology. With it, the trade-off rate is an empirical finding and finance will defend it.

5. **Objective expressed as one currency, signed by finance.** Convert conversion, product margin, service deflection, and opt-out into expected 12-month contribution margin per customer, using item 4's coefficients. Done = a one-page spec signed by finance and at least two channel owners, and at least one channel's internal scorecard restated in it. I'd deliberately not try to get all channels to sign; get the two that are losing least and let the asymmetry do the work.

6. **One optimized decision point, narrowly scoped.** Pick a single arbitration moment with fast feedback (<72h), a handful of eligible actions, and real volume — e.g. post-purchase week-one, or cart abandon across email/push/onsite. Contextual bandit there; rules everywhere else. Done = the bandit beats the incumbent rule set on item 5's objective, measured against the global holdout, with the result replicated in a second period.

What I expect to go wrong: paid media will not accept real-time suppression — audience syncs run in hours to days, so treat advertising as a budget-and-exclusion lever, not a sequencing participant, and stop pretending otherwise in the architecture diagram. Service channels will refuse to be arbitrated and they're right; inbound always wins, and the orchestration layer should listen to service rather than control it. Identity coverage will be worse than your CDP vendor's slide claims, probably 50–70% on anonymous web/app. And the real fight is item 5, not item 6 — if the exchange rate never gets signed, you'll still have shipped a suppression layer that removes most of the embarrassing contradictions, which is roughly 60% of the actual customer-visible harm.
answers.first_move: Get every outbound message any system sends to a customer written into one shared log, including the ones marketing doesn't send.
answers.hardest_part: There is no neutral party who can price one team's conversion against another team's customer fatigue, so the trade-off has to be discovered experimentally rather than agreed in a meeting.

format.label: A lullaby
format.instruction: Write it as a short lullaby: three or four gentle rhyming couplets someone could actually sing. Soft on the surface, honest underneath. The problem is still unsolved when the song ends, and the song should know it.

Hush, little journey, the channels all sing, / each one to itself, each one proud of its ping. / We're not crowning a king tonight, only a gate: / one ledger of contacts, one soft whisper—wait. / The feedback runs late and the state's full of holes, / so price what we harm before chasing the goals. / And the budgets will quarrel, the owners will fight— / no one's yet written the sum that comes right.

(Plainly: I'd skip the central optimizer everyone pitches. Start with negative control—a shared suppression and arbitration layer every channel writes to and reads from, with veto rights only. Teams will hand you the power to say no long before they hand you the power to say send. Make fatigue and contradiction the first measured outcomes, since they're observable in hours, not quarters. Only once the ledger is trusted and complete do I'd try ranking offers globally, and even then on a crude proxy objective I expect to be wrong—margin-weighted conversion minus a contact cost, tuned by holdout, not by a dashboard. What I expect to hit: ad platforms that won't take real-time suppression at useful latency, service channels that nobody models as marketing contacts at all, and a finance structure that makes a globally better outcome look like one VP losing.)
